title: Windows and Tiles
execute:
    warning: False
---

[`Patch.window`](`dascore.Patch.window`) declares windows over a patch, and what is done in them decides what comes back:

| you want | use | what comes back |
|---|---|---|
| a value per sample, from the samples around it | a reduction, such as `patch.window(time=0.1).mean()` | a patch shaped like the input |
| a transform of each window, kept as windows | [`Patch.stft`](`dascore.Patch.stft`), or [`apply`](`dascore.proc.window.PatchWindow.apply`) with `mode="stack"` | a patch with a window axis |
| each window transformed and the windows blended back | [`apply`](`dascore.proc.window.PatchWindow.apply`) | a patch shaped like the input |

Window lengths use coordinate units or samples (`samples=True`). `overlap` accepts a count, duration, percentage, or per-dimension mapping, and `step` says how far each window advances instead. A window with neither overlaps the next by half when it is blended, and advances one sample when it is reduced.

## A value for each window

A reduction gives one value for each window, labelled by one of the input's samples: the window's middle sample by default, or its first or last with `align`. With a step of one sample the result has the input's shape. A window which reaches past either end of the data is incomplete: `ends="pad"`, the default, gives it NaN, and `ends="drop"` leaves it out.

```{python}
import numpy as np

import dascore as dc

patch = dc.get_example_patch()

smooth = patch.window(time=0.01).mean()
assert smooth.shape == patch.shape

# Only the complete windows, a tenth of a second long and half that apart.
envelope = patch.window(time=0.1, step=0.05, ends="drop").max()
assert not np.isnan(envelope.data).any()

# Any function which reduces the last axis.
upper = patch.window(time=0.1, step=0.05).reduce(np.nanpercentile, 90)
```

## Tiles, blended

`apply` passes an `[n_tiles, *window]` array to a function and blends its same-shaped result with complementary tapers. An identity function reconstructs the input exactly. This example applies windowed automatic gain control:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

import dascore as dc
from dascore.units import percent

patch = dc.get_example_patch("example_event_2").pass_filter(time=(1, 300))


def agc(tiles):
    """Scale every tile to unit RMS."""
    rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(tiles**2, axis=(1, 2), keepdims=True))
    return tiles / np.where(rms > 0, rms, 1)


normalized = patch.window(time=0.02, distance=40).apply(agc)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5), sharey=True)
for ax, pa, title in zip(axes, [patch, normalized], ["band-passed", "AGC, 20 ms by 40 m"]):
    scale = np.percentile(np.abs(pa.data), 99)
    pa.viz.waterfall(ax=ax, scale=scale, scale_type="absolute", cmap="bwr")
    ax.set_title(title)
fig.tight_layout()
```

The [adaptive spectral filter](adaptive_spectral_filter.qmd) uses the same machinery with spectral weighting.

## Tiles, kept

With `mode="stack"`, tiles remain separate. Windowed dimensions become tile-center axes, `{dim}_start` and `{dim}_stop` record physical cell edges in the dimension's units, and tile samples use `{dim}_offset`. Process the stack as a patch, then [`reassemble`](`dascore.Patch.reassemble`) it. Paired physical bounds require monotonic row order; explicitly drop the public bounds before an arbitrary tile permutation. Private reconstruction indices follow the rows and still allow reassembly.

```{python}
tiles = patch.window(time=0.02, distance=40).apply(lambda x: x, mode="stack")
print(tiles.dims, tiles.shape)

# Drop every tile whose energy is in the lowest quarter, then blend back.
# The mean keeps the offset axes at length one, so a per-tile flag
# broadcasts back over every sample of its tile.
energy = (tiles**2).mean(dim=("distance_offset", "time_offset"))
quiet = energy.data < np.percentile(energy.data, 25)
kept = tiles.new(data=np.where(quiet, 0, tiles.data))
denoised = kept.reassemble()
assert denoised.shape == patch.shape
```

An unchanged stack reassembles exactly. `stft` transforms the offset axes; `istft` inverts them and reassembles.

## A compiled function, one tile at a time

A Numba-compiled function receives one tile at a time in parallel. This supports any number of dimensions and `mode="stack"`, with a one-time compilation cost per process.

```{python}
#| eval: false
import numba


@numba.njit
def agc_tile(tile):
    rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(tile * tile))
    return tile / rms if rms > 0 else tile


normalized = patch.window(time=0.02, distance=40).apply(agc_tile)
```

## A window on the way in

By default only blending is tapered. Set `analysis` to window each tile before the function; blending uses the window's dual so identity remains exact and overlap may exceed half the window.

```{python}
def keep_strongest(tiles):
    """Keep the largest quarter of each tile's f-k coefficients."""
    spectra = np.fft.rfft2(tiles)
    cutoff = np.percentile(np.abs(spectra), 75, axis=(1, 2), keepdims=True)
    return np.fft.irfft2(np.where(np.abs(spectra) < cutoff, 0, spectra), s=tiles.shape[1:])


window = patch.window(time=0.02, distance=40, analysis="hann", overlap=75 * percent)
local_fk = window.apply(keep_strongest)
assert local_fk.shape == patch.shape
```

## What a tile sees

Tiles extend before the data with zero padding so every contributing tile exists. Overlap defaults to half the window and cannot exceed half with blend-only tapers; analysis windows may overlap as far as SciPy can invert them. [`get_window`](`dascore.utils.signal.get_window`) supplies supported taper shapes.
